R A Introduction In recent years, with the increasing popularity of online learning and the transformation of teaching models, the family environment has played an increasingly important role in students' academic development. The growing integration of online and blended learning into mainstream education underscores this shift. Relevant data highlights the scale of this trend. For instance, the National Survey Report on the Application of Educational Informatization in Primary and Secondary Schools (III) released by Peking University (Ministry of Education, 2022) indicated that a significant proportion (73%) of surveyed students experienced school-arranged online classes conducted remotely from home. Parallel institutionalized mechanisms have emerged internationally to formalize this approach. Singapore's Ministry of Education (CNA, 2023) established designated "Home-Based Learning" days. All schools typically implement these approximately twice monthly, adapting to evolving digital learning paradigms and addressing personalized education needs. This reflects the expanding role of online learning modalities, which often extend into the home environment, within primary and secondary education. Previous research has shown that parental support for online learning (such as accompanying, supervising study, and assisting with homework) can positively influence students' online learning outcomes, engagement, and psychological well-being (Zhu et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2022). Additionally, creating a good learning environment (providing a quiet study space and ensuring smooth internet access) can significantly predict learning engagement, and a positive parent-child atmosphere can have a positive impact on students' psychological states during learning (Cao et al., 2022). This normal is characterized by the pursuit of mixing, integration, and symbiosis in instructional and learning processes (Li, 2020), and has facilitated the emergence of broader home-based online learning for students (Zweig et al., 2021). Nonetheless, this transition also poses considerable challenges in establishing an effective and cohesive framework for home-based online learning. With the popularization and scaling up of online instruction, some parents have encountered multifaceted challenges —spanning emotional, cognitive, behavioral, and competence-based dimensions—when supporting their children’s home-based online learning, even necessitating the development of additional pedagogical skills (Guo et al., 2024). Research has identified that parents generally lack subject knowledge and pedagogical skills in online learning contexts, with work commitments limiting their capacity for in-depth academic assistance, and home environments often lacking a conducive learning atmosphere (Isnawan et al., 2022). Similarly, students participating in online learning faced tangible obstacles, such as limited awareness of independent learning (China Institute of Education Policy Research, BNU, 2020), inadequate access to essential software and hardware resources (UNICEF, 2020; Lau and Lee, 2020), and barriers to communication and feedback (Big Data Center, Graduate School of Education, Peking University, 2020). Theoretical foundation of family support Social support theory is an important cornerstone for understanding the concept of family support (Canavan et al., 2006, pp.11-14). In the early 1970s, the concept of social support was introduced to the psychiatric literature, and sociological and medical circles developed relevant scales to study the relationship between social support and individuals’ physical and mental health. Since the beginning of the 21st century, related research in the field of education has shown an obvious upward trend, aiming to promote students’ physical and mental health and development by improving social support. Scholars have different understandings and dimensional definitions of social support, so it needs to be approached from multiple perspectives. Early research was based on understanding the nature of social support and primarily adopted a instrumental/emotional (Cutrona, 1990) or objectivity/subjectivity dichotomies (Sarason et al., 1983). With the deepening of research, researchers have gradually realized the complex relationships within social support systems, and more diverse classifications have emerged. From the perspective of source composition, some researchers havSe divided the social support provided by different groups, institutions, or individuals from macro to micro leveSls (Li, 1998; Xing and Gu, 2006). From the perspective of content composition, some researchers have derived mEore abundant forms of resource support based on earlier dichotomies, such as emotional, material, informationaRl, and companionship support (Cohen and Wills, 1985; Wellman and Wortley, 1990). Numerous studies on sociaPl support theory have clearly identified the types and characteristics of relationships that provide support in conc ise, approachable terms that can be directly applied to N the field of family support (Canavan et al., 2006, p.8). I Family structure, as a direct manifestation of familial relationships, living patterns, and household functions, refers to the interconnected relationships amonEg family members formed through bonds of kinship, marriage, legal ties, and emotional connections. It carries muLltifaceted social implications. In China, family types exhibit diversified C characteristics and cultural complexity, broadly categorized into six types: nuclear families, stem families, composite I families, single-person households, non-intact families, and others (Wang, 2013). To date, there remains no T consensus in domestic and international academia regarding the classification and nomenclature of family R structures. Due to the profound emphasis on ethical relationships in traditional Chinese family culture, Chinese A scholars prioritize generational characteristics when classifying family structures. For instance, stem families are further subdivided into two-generation stem families, three-generation stem families, four-or-more-generation stem families, and skip-generation stem families (Wang, 2024). Chinese family structures are characterized by three key trends: miniaturization of scale, nuclearization of structure, and diversification of types (Tong and Song, 2016). With the intensification of population migration and mobility, the deepening of socio-economic modernization, and the acceleration of urbanization processes, family structures in China have grown increasingly diverse and complex (Zhang and Wang, 2022). It is widely recognized that the structural integrity of families and harmonious family relationships are critical to the effective functioning of family support mechanisms (Wang, 2023). Family members are usually among the most frequent and influential sources of support for the individuals in their daily contact sphere and are also the most sustained and stable providers of individual emotional support and various material support (Canavan et al., 2000; Diao, 2012). In a home-based online learning environment, students need to manage their learning process independently, without the direct supervision and interaction of a traditional school setting, and require timely additional emotional, technical, and pedagogical assistance from parents. Current research shows that the higher the level of family support, the stronger the motivation and engagement of students for online learning (Rasyida and Hakim, 2022; Khoirunnisa and Purwandari, 2023). Specifically, family support refers to social behaviors whereby members mutually provide emotional sustenance and instrumental assistance through shared responsibilities, care, and collaborative interaction, thereby enhancing social adaptability (Yang and ARTICLE IN PRESS Xue, 2022), Canavan and Pinkerton (2006) categorize family support into emotional support, appreciation support, instrumental-concrete support, and informational support. Similarly, multidimensional frameworks classify such support as comprising emotional, instrumental, informative, and companionship support (Cohen and Wills, 1985; Wellman and Wortley, 1990; Khoirunnisa and Purwandari, 2023; Rasyida and Hakim, 2023). Jacobson (1986) synthesized stress theory with support theory, proposing complementary frameworks that classify support into three overarching types—emotional, cognitive, and material—while introducing a temporal dimension. Stress theory elucidates the emergence of stressors (e.g., when demands exceed coping capacities or remain unmet), whereas support theory conceptualizes resources that fulfill these demands. In the context of students’ home-based online learning, unrecognized or unmet academic needs may generate stress and burnout; parental involvement assists students in mitigating negative psychological states and enhancing their engagement in online learning (Zhao et al., 2022). In summary, family support, as a behavioral activity to promote students' development, provides stable and lasting support to students in various ways, such as emotional, material, cognitive, and experiential. It considers various aspects, including students' online learning psychology (e.g., mitigating loneliness and anxiety), their fundamental support needs (e.g., reliable supervision and timely homeworSk assistance),, and the real challenges faced by families in supporting students' home-based online learning (Se.g., gaps in emotional, instructional, and technical competencies). Additionally, since support unfolds or changesP over time (Jacobson, 1986), when defining family support, we have considered the stages of different types o f support. For example, emotional adaptation typically N occurs in the early stages of students' online learning at home, while reflection on quality and effectiveness usually I takes place in the middle to later stages. The specific content of experiential support and communication and interaction also varies across different stages. A Influenced by children's age, intellectual development and self-control, home-based online learning requires more help and support from parents than traditional schooling. Parents of students participating in home-based online learning must play multiple roles, such as supervisor, resource provider and companion. Therefore, they must not only provide students with equipment, technology, resources and methods for online learning but also have a deeper understanding of students' learning, communicate more with teachers, and know more about the school's arrangements and teaching progress than previously (Song et al., 2020; Ben-Amram and Davidovitch, 2021). In fact, in support of students' home-based online learning, parents need to solve more problems than first imagined. For example, the inadequate information literacy of some parents and their low willingness to communicate with teachers have become practical problems for students learning online at home (Fu and Zhou, 2020). Students' long-term use of electronic devices has also prompted parental concern about the risk of internet addiction and vision deterioration (Yu and Wang, 2020). In addition to education-related tasks, parents must also attend to housework and their own work, which inevitably leads to confusion. Therefore, parents are faced with problems such as a lack of time and energy, limited educational ability, insufficient understanding of online learning and excessive worry. Sometimes, they are overwhelmed by having taken on excessive tasks from the school. For example, many schools and teachers have transferred the supervision of students' learning largely to parents. They require parents to take and upload photos, record attendance and register for classes, and document students' learning; this shift reflects the influence of "trace doctrine" and "formalism" (Jiao et al., 2020). In this context, the ARTICLE IN PRESS problem of home-school cooperation has become increasingly prominent. Although most parents and teachers agree on the need for home-school cooperation, some teachers believe that the boundaries of responsibility should be drawn differently, and some parents have expressed their disapproval of at-home education (Zhang et al., 2020). This divergence to some extent reflects a lack of cooperative awareness. The so-called “cooperative awareness” involves not only parents' and teachers' recognition of the importance of cooperation but also their willingness and ability to actively participate in it. For example, in students' online learning at home, the transformation of trust relationships in home-school cooperation (Zheng and Wan, 2020), the lack of teacher feedback, support, and communication (Guo et al., 2024), and the deficiency in parents' and teachers' coordination and communication skills (Fu and Zhou, 2020) may erode the cooperative awareness of both parties. In addition, online teaching has made collaboration more difficult, leading to the magnification of differences in the quality and efficiency of online teaching due to regional and family environment factors (Hu et al., 2020). Parental difficulties have resulted in a snowball-like chain reaction. In summary, four main difficulties in family support of students' home-based online learning are identified. First of all, parents' time and energy are difficult to coordinate and balance. Furthermore, parents' information literacy level and communication ability are limited. Overall, the total score for family support was 3.57, situated between "neutral" and "basically consistent," indicating a moderately high level of overall support provided by families for students' online learning at home. However, this support was not uniformly distributed across its specific dimensions. Specifically, communication and interaction emerged as the core facet of family support, yielding the highest dimension score (M=4.16, SD=0.56). This reflects families' active engagement with students' specific learning needs during online study, manifested through frequent parent-child interactions, close home-school collaboration, and the timely resolution of learning difficulties. The score for experiential support was the next highest (M=3.88, SD=0.73), signifying families' significant prioritization of providing scaffolding experience and assistance for students' home-based online learning. In contrast, significantly lower scores were obtained for emotional adaptation (M=3.12, SD=0.75), revealing insufficient parental attention to students' anxiety and adaptation difficulties during online learning, coupled with relatively limited emotional companionship. The lowest score was observed for reflection on quality and effectiveness (M=2.84, SD=0.86), indicating a widespread lack of deep critical reflection within families on the value, quality, and effectiveness of the home- based online learning experience; specifically, parents infrequently assessed student learning outcomes, reflected on goal attainment, or considered strategies for enhancing efficiency and quality. Discussion Lack of Self-Regulation Leads to Emotional Maladjustment. "Self-regulation ability" or "emotional control ability" are important educational abilities that help parents actively regulate their own emotional changes and prepare for family education (Cai, 2013, p.47; Huang, 2014, p.92). This study revealed that parents' emotional maladjustment was more prominent in families with less daily education duration investment and families with lower parental educational attainment. Firstly of all, even more than economic investment, education duration investment serves as the critical determinant influencing children's academic performance (Li and He, 2019), playing an indispensable role in student development. A large-scale survey of 200,000 U.S. households revealed that during home-based online learning periods, 72% of parents invested 2.6 hours per school day supporting their children's education—though this increased time commitment may entail employment or income sacrifices (Bansak and Starr, 2021).Within China's universal two-child policy context, this tension manifests most acutely as chronic time scarcity and energy depletion among parents, where resultant unequal time distribution generates disruptive household dynamics that ultimately affect parental mood (Sun, 2017). Secondly, parental educational attainment directly shapes the familial psychological environment, as parents ARTICLE IN PRESS with higher qualifications demonstrate stronger educational awareness and more proactive pedagogical approaches (Cai, 2013, p.47). In our investigation, low-attainment parents manifested significantly lower acceptance of home- based online teaching during initial implementation phases and greater propensity for negative educational attitudes compared to their high-attainment counterparts. However, this finding diverges from Addi-Raccah's (2024) conclusion that while low-SES parents may possess fewer resources, they actively leverage diversified capital forms to support children's learning—a compensatory dynamic that may potentially account for overlooked dimensions of parental agency and positive educational attitudes among less-educated families in our study. Finally, the problem of parents' emotional maladjustment manifests primarily in the early and middle stages of students' at-home online learning. In the early stage, most parental concerns focused on three aspects: the need for non-only-child families to coordinate class schedules, the impact of online learning on students' vision, and insufficient student self-motivation. Parents also demonstrated lower acceptance of electronic products and information technology than students did (Li and He, 2019), so students' online learning may prompt anxiety for parents (Fu and Zhou, 2020). Parents instinctively develop negative attitudes toward unfamiliar and "potentially hazardous" situations (Garbe et al., 2020); failure to positively regulate these reactions can trigger emotional maladjustment (Sandberg et al.,2025). In the middle stage, most parents exprSessed concern about students’ learning effectiveness. Deeply influenced by traditional Chinese Confucian princiSples such as "learning excellence leads to officialdom" (学而优则仕), parents maintain heightened expectatioEns that transcend academic achievement to encompass moral development and social mobility (Huang andR Gove, 2015; Sheng, 2019). Empirical research further indicates that Chinese parents must mitigate their owPn educational anxiety to effectively support children in overcoming online learning burnout (Zhao et al., 2022). In our research, three student interviewees shared similar N views on their parents' academic support during home-based online learning: "When I was in a math course online, I I’ve noticed that there are the questions the teacher has explained multiple times, but I still can’t grasp it. My mother scolded me, which made me angry! Even for somEe of the questions, she doesn’t know how to solve them!” (62-X2G3); "My mother also scolded me sometimes becLause I couldn't finish tasks and made mistakes” (63-X1G3); and "Yes, C extremely frustrating!” (64-X3G3). These accounts substantiate Boonk et al.'s (2018) literature review findings: I educators, parents, and researchers should not assume all forms of parental involvement are inherently beneficial. T This is particularly critical regarding homework assistance, where certain parental engagement approaches may R prove ineffective or even contribute to academic regression. A Constraints on the Time and Energy Leads to Inadequate Experiential Support. Parents’ attentive accompaniment of students is also more important than economic investment for student growth and development. This study revealed that parents provided insufficient experiential support, which was more prominent in families with less education duration investment and families with lower parental educational attainment. Firstly of all, the duration of family education investment is likely to affect the frequency and amount of experiential support. Only-child families invested significantly more time in family education than non-only-child families (Gu et al., 2021), which may be due to difficulties with parental energy input in families with more children. This pattern aligns with international findings demonstrating a positive correlation between the number of school- aged children and parental burnout, where child-rearing demands significantly contribute to elevated burnout levels (Teuber et al., 2023). Critically, each additional child substantially increases risks of parental emotional exhaustion, exposing multi-child families to heightened depletion of emotional resources (Mikolajczak and Roskam, 2018). Simultaneously, parents with fewer children typically experience lower stress levels during online learning periods, correlating with higher perceived satisfaction with remote education (Lau et al., 2021). Conversely, parents experiencing greater stress often feel overwhelmed by online learning challenges, struggling to identify appropriate academic support strategies or effectively address their children's concerns and anxieties (Spinelli et al., 2020). Secondly, parental educational attainment also potentially influences experiential support. Parents holding ARTICLE IN PRESS higher education attainment tend to invest greater energy in implementing democratic, scientifically grounded, and pedagogically appropriate educational approaches, thereby positively impacting children's academic outcomes (Fang and Feng, 2008; Žerak et al., 2024). Conversely, parents experiencing lower socioeconomic status encounter significant involvement barriers—including demanding work schedules, time constraints, and limited access to educational resources—that may fundamentally compromise their involvement in children's online learning (Suryadi et al., 2023). Finally, parental experiential support differs based on parental versus instructional perspectives. While most families expressed confidence in addressing students' academic and technical difficulties, recurrent demands for learning assistance (e.g., troubleshooting homework) precipitated emotional exhaustion among some parents, thereby constraining their capacity to deliver sustained practical support. Teachers, in contrast, wanted parents to devote more time and energy to students' home-based online learning and to provide children with more experiential support. Regarding the provision of experiential support, one teacher stated bluntly that "parents should naturally shoulder the responsibility of supervision and companionship during online learning, and they need to be aware of their children's learning progress. For instance, while we advocate 'identifying gaps and making up for shortcomings' in student learning, some parents remain unaware oSf these gaps—how then can they help students address them?”(10-BF4). This reflects the misalignment betSween teacher expectations and parental capabilities: teachers anticipate parents becoming curricular co-imEplementers rather than mere supervisors. However, existing research also indicates students demonstrateR inattention and low motivation when taught by parents as temporary instructors, while parents themselves oPften struggle when explaining new curricular topics (Mifsud, 2021). N I Weak Awareness of Observation Leads to Poor Reflection on Quality and Effectiveness. As a parental educational ability, observation helps parents Egrasp students' needs and educational opportunities in a timely manner (Cai, 2013, p.45) to help them reflecLt on the quality and effectiveness of their child’s education. This study C revealed that parents struggle with reflection and that this problem is more prominent in non-only-child families, I families with less daily education duration investment, and families with lower parental educational attainment. T Firstly, following the initiation of China's universal two-child policy, the structure of children within families R has changed considerably. Compared with only-child families, non-only-child families are more likely to experience A confusion and chaos, which consume much of the opportunity and time parents need to observe and reflect on education. However, some research has also found a weak negative correlation between the number of children and parental involvement, suggesting no significant difference in parental involvement between only-child families and families with multiple children (Shao et al., 2022). Such discrepancies in findings may stem from differences in the dimensions encompassed by parental involvement in those studies versus the concept of family support examined here. Parental involvement typically includes dimensions such as study guidance and psychological counseling, whereas the family support construct in this study encompasses a broader range of aspects related to parental engagement. Secondly, the potential positive impact of parental reflection on family support requires parents to emphasize daily observation of students. This relates to the finding that the more time students spend with their parents, the more conducive it is to improving family intimacy and optimizing students' learning effectiveness (Sun, 2017). Furthermore, existing research also indicates that parents exhibiting high levels of involvement hold more positive perceptions of online education quality, as their in-depth involvement enhances understanding of the teaching and learning process (Shao et al., 2022). Thirdly, parents with lower education levels are less likely to reflect on the quality and effectiveness of at-home online teaching. This limitation arises because parental cooperation in online environments demands specific knowledge, abilities, and information literacy (Hu et al., 2020). According to Hou and Tian (2021), pre-existing ARTICLE IN PRESS advantages or disadvantages in parental cultural capital are thereby converted into latent disparities in their digital teaching literacy. Therefore, parents with lower educational attainment may face significant challenges in participating effectively in their children’s home-based online learning. This difficulty increases their likelihood of inadequately monitoring learning progress, which in turn compromises accurate assessment of their children’s academic quality and effectiveness. Finally, parents without professional teaching backgrounds demonstrate greater difficulty in engaging with reflection on the quality and effectiveness of online learning. Previous studies have established that parents' professional status significantly influences their educational participation (Tian and Qi, 2004; Wang, 2012). Our findings further indicate that professional identity substantially shapes capacity for reflection on quality and effectiveness. Parents with teaching occupations possess a dual identity that enables them to more readily examine instructional processes and learning outcomes during online education (Hungo et al., 2025). Moreover, large-scale online teaching objectively affords these teacher-parents more robust family support resources. This aligns with Antony-Newman et al.'s (2023) observation that parental teaching expertise facilitates systematic organization of comprehensive homeschooling and strategic application of pedagogical experience to address knowledge gaps. N A Lack of Clarity on Family-School Responsibilities Hinders Family Support. Research demonstrates that a I positive alignment of attitudes toward online learning between teachers and parents yields constructive impacts (Shamma, 2024). Furthermore, high-quality pEarent-teacher collaboration can prevent parental burnout while potentially enhancing parental engagementL (Teuber et al., 2024), ultimately providing long-term benefits for C students' academic growth (Darling-Hammond et al., 2019). However, students' home-based online learning has I triggered escalating academic responsibilities and intensified conflicts between families and schools. Blurred T boundaries and overlapping responsibilities leave parents without clear guidance, while incompatible expectations R between parents and teachers—compounded by insufficient timely feedback—hinder effective home-school A collaboration, ultimately impeding students' access to family support. The interview data enabled us to clarify the division of responsibilities between families and schools at both the factual and normative levels and to further examine the underlying reasons for challenges in providing family support. The factual level refers to the support provided by parents and teachers in the process of students' home- based online learning. Parents provide family support mainly through experiential support. In contrast, teachers primarily help students with online teaching through two types of activities: knowledge transmission and methods instruction. Specific instructional practices included creating "microlectures", teaching students online learning methods and guiding their use (4-AF1), establishing a subject preparation group to discuss teaching collectively (6- CF2; 6-DF2), designing online learning groups to let parents and students participate in learning activities (25-EF3), and combining online courses and videos in their online teaching (7-EF3). The normative level refers to the expectations parents and teachers hold of each other concerning students' home-based online learning. Parents believed that teachers should provide support principally in the aspects of supervision and teaching, while teachers suggested three aspects of their expectations of parents: "supervision and accompaniment", "implementation and uploading of learning tasks", and "mastering students’ learning". Based on the cross-boundary cooperation between home and school led by the current school (Wu, 2018; Zhang et al., 2018), on the one hand, this surge in short-term tasks is likely to arouse negative parental emotions and affect family support. On the other hand, parents' lack of understanding of teachers' online teaching work easily ARTICLE IN PRESS leads to misunderstandings and affects home-school cooperation. As evidenced by the current exploration of family- school responsibility boundaries (Kang, 2019), on the one hand, teachers believed that parents need to undertake more detailed supervision and implementation than usual in students' home-based online learning. On the other hand, parents believed that teachers needed to consider students' learning needs more carefully in their instructional design. As reflected in these teacher and parent perspectives, the expectations of these groups become trapped in a difficult cycle due to a lack of timely negotiation and adjustment. Conclusions and Suggestions In the context of large-scale online teaching, the dilemma of family support of students' home-based online learning concerns parents' poor reflection on quality and effectiveness, emotional maladjustment, insufficient experiential support, and unclear responsibility allocation between home and school. In addition, students' family support and levels of all dimensions are affected by family roles, number of children, daily education duration investment, and parents' highest degree obtained. The theoretical contribution of this study lies in integrating multi-stakeholder perspectives to reveal limitations and inherent tensions in family support within technology-empowered learning environments, systematically identifying core dimensions and key constraiSnts of family support for home-based online learning. This provides a conceptual framework for understanSding mechanisms through which family support enables sustainable student development. Therefore, parents may need to undertake more basic supervision and implementation work, while teachers may need to consider students' learning needs more carefully and enhance student monitoring and interaction. To improve home-school cooperation, the two sides need to exchange views in a timely manner and respond to needs and expectations to promote the mutual distribution of responsibilities in specific situations. For instance, developing standardized home-school responsibility benchmarks can clarify operational demarcation between families and schools for specific online learning tasks. Moreover, parents and teachers should not only focus on the achievement of their respective tasks but also attempt to avoid the phenomena of "responsibility dispersion" and "work duplication" stemming from task overlap. Consequently, establishing categorized home-school communication models becomes necessary to delineate core obligations for each party, thereby reducing intervention redundancies. Another important point is enabling mutual assistance between families and schools through bidirectional commitment. Family-school cooperation requires schools to fully integrate disadvantaged families while each household must actively enhance participation. Limitations. This study adopted a mixed research methodology aiming to explore the current status, challenges, and underlying reasons for family support. However, there remain some limitations. In the first place, the "reflection on quality and effectiveness" dimension has a relatively low reliability coefficient, which may be because (1) there are few relevant scales to refer to, so this study adopted a newly self- generated scale to investigate this topic; (2) the dimension includes only three items; and (3) the results of the self- ARTICLE IN PRESS report scale are influenced by random errors such as participant emotions or contexts. Nevertheless, this study retained this dimension because the level of parents’ reflection on quality and effectiveness exerts a considerable impact on students’ home-based online learning. Thus, this study supplemented and improved the content of this dimension through interviews. Moving on to the next point, the researchers ensured the quality and reliability of the interview results through two approaches: (1) The researchers conducted tests and revised the interview outline and (2) this study employed data triangulation to validate the research findings. For example, regarding parental emotional maladjustment, the interview process revealed attitudes shared directly by parents, supplemented by examples from students and insights from teachers. However, this study focused specifically on parents who faced difficulties in providing support, which allowed a detailed diagnosis of challenges but limited our ability to contrast these with successful cases. Future research could include high-support families to identify enabling factors and validate the barriers identified here. Meanwhile, the small number of participants, especially teachers, somewhat overlooked the diversity of teacher participants and limited the interpretive power and generalizability of the qualitative data. In the future, the questionnaire design and the number of interview participants in this study need further revision and improvement to fully include teachers from different backgrounds, schooSls, or teaching experiences. Moreover, subsequent investigations should incorporate additional influential factoSrs such as household economic conditions, while implementing child-parent paired sampling approaches to Eenhance sampling representativity, thereby ensuring comprehensive and scientifically robust conclusions aboRut family support research. Finally, the ‘skip-generation child-rearing’ pattern, in wPhich grandparents are involved in child-rearing in Chinese families, may have a significant impact on the level of family education support. JSON: Name: family_support_online_learning_pipeline Title: A mixed-methods study and experimental pipeline to identify causal pathways through which family support dimensions affect the sustainability of primary students' home-based online learning Short Hypothesis: Lower parental time investment and lower parental digital/pedagogical competence cause reduced sustainability of students' home-based online learning, as measured by decreased student engagement and lower learning gains. Related Work: Existing research on family involvement in online K-12 learning primarily follows two strands: (1) controlled experimental and quantitative studies that evaluate instructional modalities, teacher-led interventions, and student learning outcomes in restricted environments; and (2) cross-sectional surveys and qualitative reports that document parental attitudes, infrastructure gaps, and descriptive associations between parental involvement and student outcomes. Limitations across prior approaches include heavy reliance on laboratory-like or teacher-centric settings (weak external validity for home contexts), predominantly correlational analyses that do not identify causal mechanisms, coarse measurement of parental support (focus on time or resources but not multidimensional constructs such as emotional adaptation, experiential support, communication, and reflective practice), sparse multi-stakeholder triangulation, and limited use of clustered or hierarchical models to control for school/class-level confounds. Few studies combine validated measurement models with causal designs (e.g., cluster randomization, mediation analysis) to test which parental support dimensions drive sustainable learning outcomes over time. Abstract: Problem: Families are critical for sustaining primary students' home-based online learning, but parental support often fails to produce persistent engagement and measurable learning gains. Approach: This pipeline integrates psychometric scale construction, observational modeling, and a cluster-randomized pilot intervention to test causal links among parental time investment, parental digital/pedagogical competence, emotional adaptation, experiential support, communication patterns, and student outcomes. Main contribution: (1) a validated four-dimension family-support measurement model for home-based online learning; (2) an observational multilevel analysis identifying direct and mediated predictors of engagement and learning gains; and (3) a cluster-randomized trial evaluating a targeted parental-training+communication protocol and estimating average treatment effects and mediation pathways. Expected outcome: precise identification of which actionable parental support dimensions causally influence sustainable online learning, quantified effect sizes, and an evidence-informed intervention blueprint for schools and policymakers. Experiments: Phase 1 — Measurement and observational modeling: dataset A = existing survey (n=508 parents) and interview transcripts (n≈28). Conduct confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to validate four latent factors: emotional_adaptation, experiential_support, communication_interaction, reflection_quality. Compute reliability (Cronbach's alpha, omega) and factor scores. Fit multilevel mixed-effects regressions (random intercepts for school/class) predicting student engagement_index and pre/post learning_gain using covariates: student grade, gender, family_type, number_of_children, parental_education, daily_education_duration. Report standardized betas, 95% CIs, p-values. Perform mediation analysis to test whether parental competence mediates the effect of time_investment on outcomes. Ablation: re-fit models excluding each latent factor sequentially to estimate marginal contributions (ΔR2, change in AIC/BIC). Phase 2 — Cross-sectional replication: collect dataset B: stratified sample across 12 primary schools, target n=1800 parent-student pairs; include baseline standardized pretest and posttest (subject-specific), device access, and logged engagement (attendance, time-on-task). Re-run CFA and multilevel models; compare model fit and effect-size replication versus dataset A. Phase 3 — Cluster randomized pilot (causal test): recruit 24 classes (clusters) across 8 schools, average cluster size ≈20 students, total N≈480. Randomize clusters 1:1 to intervention vs control. Intervention = 8-week parental training (four 60-min modules: digital facilitation, pedagogical scaffolding, emotional regulation, home-school communication) + standardized teacher-parent communication protocol; control = status quo. Primary outcomes: student learning_gain (standardized test pre→post), engagement_index (logged attendance, assignment completion rate), self_regulated_learning_score (validated scale). Secondary outcomes: parental_reflection_score, parent_teach_competence_score, teacher-reported student behavior. Analysis: intention-to-treat mixed-effects regression with random intercepts for cluster and school; estimate average treatment effect (ATE) and cluster-robust SEs. Mediation: test whether changes in parental_competence and time_investment mediate ATE on learning_gain using multilevel structural equation modeling. Power: design powered to detect ATE Cohen's d≈0.35 assuming ICC=0.05, alpha=0.05, 80% power (24 clusters × ~20 students). Comparisons and ablations: (a) baseline model vs model adding parental competence and emotional adaptation; (b) intervention vs active-waitlist control (if implemented); (c) subgroup analyses by parental education and number_of_children. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement and self-report bias: parental and student self-reports may over- or under-estimate actual behaviors; social desirability and recall bias affect scale scores. Causal identification limits: observational phases remain vulnerable to unobserved confounding; cluster RCT pilot may still have contamination or noncompliance. External validity: samples drawn from a limited geographic/cultural context (Chongqing region) may not generalize to other regions or age groups. Sample size and clustering: cluster RCT power depends on ICC and cluster sizes; higher ICCs or attrition will reduce power. Intervention uptake: variable parent participation and differential adherence will attenuate treatment effects. Psychometrics: the reflection_on_quality factor may show lower reliability if items are few or heterogenous. Data missingness and attrition: longitudinal pre/post measures subject to dropout; missing-not-at-random patterns may bias estimates. Ethical/privacy constraints: collecting fine-grained engagement logs and family data raises privacy and consent burdens. Scalability: implementing the parental training intervention at scale requires resources and teacher capacity not modeled here. Cultural specificity: parental roles, family structure (e.g., skip-generation caregiving) and normative expectations differ across societies, limiting generalization beyond similar contexts.
